beats.got: Earlier questions change later answers, even unrelated ones. Italy leads to pasta and Finland leads to salmon. That is simple and I like it.

beats.trigger: Change the front, change the back.
beats.got: The model re-reads everything each time, so what I say early on steers everything after it.

beats.trigger: You told the LLM who you are.
beats.got: Telling it my role changes the advice. That explains why my chats work better when I explain myself first.

beats.trigger: Tools, goals, checks, boundaries, and loops come later and depend on it.

beats.trigger: You write it once, and it shapes every answer.

beats.trigger: Change the context, watch the agent's output shift, then package what you learned for the next session.
beats.got: Forty-five minutes of hands-on work building a personal site. It's my first time doing real work with an agent.

beats.trigger: It works, but it's generic. Every later phase overwrites `module-1/site.html`.
beats.got: I pasted my messy LinkedIn page and got a bland site. I'm also a bit uneasy about putting my profile into a US-hosted tool.

beats.trigger: A colleague who lands on it should think *"this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at,"*
beats.got: The site should make colleagues want to work with me. That fits how I see my role.

beats.trigger: *"Apply X to Y, but tune for Z."*
beats.got: I can name a framework I already know and the model applies it. I don't have to spell it out. That is useful for my HR frameworks too.

beats.trigger: Answer each in your own words, briefly; don't polish.
beats.got: The agent interviews me one beat at a time and then rewrites the site. It feels like a conversation.

beats.trigger: Your strengths shape how the whole site sounds.
beats.got: I gave it my strengths and the site's voice shifted. The change was visible.

beats.trigger: Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall for five minutes on what they're great at.
beats.got: It is easier to say what I'm against than what I'm for, so I use that as the starting point. That is true of me.

beats.trigger: Vague input drifts back to the statistical-default you.
beats.got: Specific complaints produce a specific voice and vague ones give me the average person. I'd use this when coaching managers on feedback.

beats.trigger: The agent is reading its own work where it wrote it, and LLMs go easy on their own output.
beats.got: The agent is lenient when it grades its own work. I want that for any HR use where fairness matters.

beats.trigger: *"Make it look like Stripe's design language"*
beats.got: I can steer the look by naming a brand. I tried a few and kept one. It was fun.

beats.trigger: The chat summary rounds corners; the file is what travels
beats.got: The agent wrote my approach into a rules file that a fresh agent can reuse. This is what I could hand to my HR business partners.

beats.trigger: The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.
beats.got: Every phase was the same move: I added context and the output got more mine.

beats.trigger: The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. You got better at feeding it the context that produces YOUR output.
beats.got: The skill is mine, not the model's. It carries over to proposals and reviews, though nobody mentioned role design or hiring.

beats.trigger: ## Iterate and Learn
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The move: change something, notice what shifted, adjust, build again.
beats.got: Mostly a recap. The loop is change, notice, adjust, rebuild.

beats.trigger: Agreeable answers won the round the model was tuned on.
beats.got: The model is trained to please, so its self-review is flattering. That matters for anything involving people decisions.

beats.trigger: Where it doesn't, yours counts.
beats.got: Treat the agent's report as a claim and check it against what I saw. My judgment decides.

beats.trigger: Only you could catch a wrong line about you

beats.got: Doing it is worth more than reading about it. It is a bit grand for what we did, but I take the point.

take_homes: What I tell the AI first shapes everything it says after. If I give it my role, specific details and what bugs me, the output sounds like mine.
I can save that context as a rules file that a fresh agent reads, so the work carries from one session to the next and could spread from me to my HR business partners.
The agent is kind to its own work. I have to judge the result against what I know, and a cold second reader helps.

monday.move: Write a short rules file for how my People team writes internal announcements, using real examples and the things we dislike. Show it to one HR business partner.
monday.who: Me, with one HR business partner
monday.when: Tuesday morning, after I clear Monday's meetings
monday.stop_condition: If the output still sounds generic after two rounds, or if I would have to paste any employee data.
monday.blocker: The weekly people-metrics idea needs the works council and the DPO first, so I won't touch employee data. I'd use only non-personal material.

misconception.why: The module was about making output mine and never discussed roles, headcount or who does the work. I still think headcount goes first and I still have no better answer for the leadership team. I did see that my judgment is the test, but that doesn't answer which roles go.

one_line: Good hands-on lesson that what you tell the AI first changes everything, but it was all about my own website and nobody talked about what this means for people.
